blocks.prompt: The Owl That Flies Without a Sound
blocks.text: An owl has a soft feather coat. Every flying feather has a fluffy edge. The fluffy edges break up the air, so the owl makes no sound when it flies. A mouse in the grass never hears it coming. An owl cannot roll its eyes. Its eyes are stuck in place, like two flashlights pointed straight ahead. So the owl turns its whole head instead. It can turn its head far enough to look right over its own back. Then it turns it back the other way. Some owls have two pointy tufts on top. Those are not ears. Those are just feathers standing up.

blocks.prompt: Why an Owl Turns Its Head
blocks.text: An owl cannot move its eyes. Most animals roll their eyes to look around, but an owl's eyes are not round like ours. They are long tubes, and they are locked into rings of bone in its skull. An owl looking straight ahead is stuck looking straight ahead. So the owl moves its head instead. It has fourteen bones in its neck. You have seven. All those extra bones let an owl swing its head about three quarters of the way around, far enough to look right over its own back. It does not spin its head in a full circle. It turns, it looks, and it turns back. The owl's other secret is silence. Look closely at the front edge of an owl's wing feather and you will see a row of tiny teeth, like a comb. The comb breaks the rushing air into small swirls. A soft fringe on the back edge and velvety down on top soak up the rest of the noise. A mouse in the grass hears nothing coming. By the time it looks up, the owl has already arrived.

blocks.prompt: The Face That Listens
blocks.text: A barn owl can catch a mouse in a room with no light at all. It does not need to see the mouse. It needs to hear it. Look at a barn owl's face. That pale heart shape is not decoration. It is a dish. Stiff feathers around the rim curve forward and funnel sound inward toward the ear openings hidden under the feathers on each side. The owl can even adjust those feathers to sharpen the focus, the way you cup a hand behind your ear. Then comes the strange part. The two ear openings are not level. On many owls, one sits higher on the skull than the other, and one points slightly down while the other points slightly up. That crookedness is the whole trick. A sound coming from below reaches the lower ear a fraction of an instant sooner, and slightly louder. A sound from above reaches the higher ear first. The owl's brain compares the two signals and reads the difference as a direction: up or down, left or right. The gap it measures is a few millionths of a second. The great gray owl takes this further. It hunts voles it has never seen, tunneling under a foot of snow, and drops through the crust feet first onto a target it located by ear alone. Owls also swallow their catch whole and cough up a neat gray pellet of bone and fur a few hours later. Pull one apart and you can read the owl's dinner, skull by skull.

blocks.prompt: The Experiment in the Dark Room
blocks.text: In the 1960s a biologist named Roger Payne wanted to settle an old argument. Everyone agreed barn owls hunted at night. Nobody agreed on how. Perhaps they saw by starlight. Perhaps they smelled the mouse, or felt its body heat, the way a snake does. Payne decided to remove every possibility but one. He built a room and sealed it against light. Not dim light. No light: no window, no crack, no glow. He released a mouse onto the leaf litter of the floor, and he waited. The owl struck it. That ruled out sight, but not smell or heat. So Payne ran the test that made the experiment famous. He tied a crumpled paper leaf to a string and dragged it across the floor. Paper has no smell a mouse would have. Paper is room temperature. The owl struck the paper. It was listening, and only listening. Later work measured how well. A barn owl can locate a sound to within one or two degrees, horizontally and vertically, which is the sharpest directional hearing ever recorded in a land animal. Two features make it possible. The first is the face: a shallow dish of stiff feathers that gathers faint sound and funnels it toward the ears. The second is that the ears are deliberately mismatched. One opening sits higher than the other and aims slightly differently, so a sound arriving from above hits the higher ear a few tens of millionths of a second sooner. Level ears could only tell left from right. Crooked ears map height as well, and the owl reads the room in three dimensions. There is one more piece, and it is the piece people misunderstand. An owl's wing is quiet because of a comb of stiff teeth along its leading edge, a soft fringe behind, and velvety down across the surface. The usual explanation is stealth, so the mouse never hears death coming. That is true, and it is only half the answer. A mouse shifting in dry grass is a whisper. An owl flapping beside its own ears would drown that whisper out completely. The silence is not only a disguise. It is the quiet the owl needs in order to hear.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Tubular eyes fixed in bony sclerotic rings
14 cervical vertebrae; arteries run slack in wide channels
Asymmetrical ears resolve sound to 1 or 2 degrees
Wing serrations damp noise above 2000 hertz
Fish owls have largely lost the serrations
Turbine blades now copy the owl's trailing edge

blocks.prompt: The Owl Is Not Wise. It Is Finished.
blocks.text: Wisdom is the one quality an owl is famous for and the one quality it does not particularly have. Ancient Athens set an owl beside its goddess of wisdom and stamped the bird on its silver coins, and the picture has held for two and a half thousand years. Test an owl against a crow or a parrot on a puzzle, though, and the owl loses badly. Crows bend wire into hooks. Parrots work through a row of locks in the correct order. Owls, handed the same problems, mostly stare. The reason is not stupidity. It is specialization. An owl's skull is a machine built for a single task, and nearly every part of it has been surrendered to that task. Start with the eyes, which are not eyeballs. They are long tubes, densely packed with light-gathering cells and wedged into rings of bone. A tube collects more light than a ball of the same weight, which is exactly what a night hunter wants. It also cannot roll. An owl's eyes are aimed permanently forward, so the owl swivels its head instead, roughly 270 degrees, on a neck carrying fourteen vertebrae where you carry seven. A turn that severe would kill most animals by pinching shut the arteries feeding the brain. The owl's neck bones are drilled with channels far wider than the arteries threaded through them, leaving the vessels slack enough to twist, and reservoirs hold a supply of blood pooled through the turn. Now the ears, which are the real instrument. The flat face is a dish. Stiff rim feathers gather faint sound and funnel it toward two openings that, in barn owls and several other species, sit at different heights and aim in different directions. That asymmetry converts a flat left-right comparison into a three-dimensional fix. The brain reads arrival-time gaps measured in tens of millionths of a second and resolves a sound to within a degree or two, the sharpest directional hearing ever measured in a land animal. In 1971 the biologist Roger Payne demonstrated what it was for. He released a mouse into a room sealed against every trace of light, and the owl struck it. Then he dragged a crumpled paper leaf across the floor on a string. The owl struck the leaf. It was not seeing, not smelling, not sensing heat. It was listening. Which brings us to the wings, and to the point most people miss. Owl flight feathers carry a comb of stiff serrations along the leading edge, a soft fringe along the trailing edge, and a velvety coat across the surface. Together they break up the turbulence that makes a wingbeat audible, especially above about 2000 hertz. The obvious explanation is stealth, and it is half right. The other half is that a mouse shifting in dry grass is an extremely quiet thing, and an owl beating its own wings beside its own ears would mask it entirely. The owl is not merely hiding from the mouse. It is manufacturing the silence in which the mouse can be heard. The proof sits in the exception. Fish owls hunt by watching water, and a fish does not hear a bird coming through the air. Fish owls have largely abandoned the serrations. The equipment appears precisely where it pays and vanishes where it does not, which is how you learn what a structure is actually for. Engineers noticed. Serrated trailing edges borrowed from owl wings now quiet the blades of wind turbines. So the owl on the coin was never the thinker Athens took it for. It is something less flattering and far more impressive: a bird with almost nothing left over, every spare part traded away for the ability to find one small sound in the dark and arrive at it unheard.
